Root

ROOT (rhymes with boot) · noun

Hear It

What It Means

The deep cause or starting point that a problem or situation grew from.

Poor communication was the root of most of the club's problems.

Worked Example

When the garden club kept missing deadlines, Ana dug past the excuses to the root: no one had ever been put in charge.

The missed deadlines were only what showed on the surface. Having no leader was the buried cause underneath, feeding every other problem - and that is what makes it the root.

How Root Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

origin

origin: the point where something first began

source

source: the place or person something comes from

cause

cause: anything that makes something happen

Antonyms

result

result: what comes out at the end of a chain of events

outcome

outcome: the way things finally turn out

How Strong Is It? — reason → root → core

reason vs. root

reason vs. root: A reason is weaker than a root: a reason is one explanation among several for what happened, while the root is the single deep cause the whole problem grew from.

core vs. root

core vs. root: Core goes further than root: the root is the buried cause a problem grew from, but the core is the very center of the whole matter, with everything else wrapped around it.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — root

root — root: the hidden underground part of a plant that feeds everything above it

Put it together

Put it together: Root has no smaller parts: the whole word is the root. English took the plant picture - the hidden part underground that feeds everything above - and used it for problems and ideas: the root of a problem is the buried cause the rest grew from.

Use the root in a new word: uproot

Use the root in a new word: uproot: The storm was strong enough to uproot the old oak, pulling it out of the ground it had grown in for a century.

Root Check

Word Choice

Reach for root when you mean the deep cause a problem grew from: writers say 'the root of the trouble' or 'get to the root of it.' Do not confuse it with onset, also taught in this unit: the root is where trouble comes from, while the onset is when it begins. Ask 'what fed this?' for root and 'when did it arrive?' for onset.
